claim: The human superior temporal plane displays high inter-individual macro-anatomical variation.
source: The human superior temporal plane, the site of the auditory cortex, displays high inter-individual macro-anatomical variation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of the superior temporal plane.

claim: High inter-individual macro-anatomical variation questions the validity of curvature-based alignment (CBA) methods for in vivo imaging data.
source: The human superior temporal plane, the site of the auditory cortex, displays high inter-individual macro-anatomical variation. This questions the validity of curvature-based alignment (CBA) methods for in vivo imaging data.
evidence: This is a logical inference presented in the abstract based on the high variability of the superior temporal plane.

claim: CBA+ is a cortical surface registration method that uses prior macro-anatomical knowledge.
source: Here, we have addressed this issue by developing CBA+, which is a cortical surface registration method that uses prior macro-anatomical knowledge.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the method developed in the study.

claim: The study validated CBA+ using cytoarchitectonic areas on 10 individual brains.
source: We validate this method by using cytoarchitectonic areas on 10 individual brains (which we make publicly available).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the validation approach used in the study.

claim: CBA+ results in a more accurate cytoarchitectonic auditory atlas compared to volumetric and standard surface registration.
source: Compared to volumetric and standard surface registration, CBA+ results in a more accurate cytoarchitectonic auditory atlas.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Improved alignment of macro-anatomy results in improved correspondence of micro-anatomy.
source: The improved correspondence of micro-anatomy following the improved alignment of macro-anatomy validates the superiority of CBA+ compared to CBA.
evidence: This is a key conclusion stated in the abstract and demonstrated through the study's results.

claim: CBA+ was used to align in vivo and postmortem data.
source: In addition, we use CBA+ to align in vivo and postmortem data.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an application of the method.

claim: Aligning in vivo and postmortem data allows projection of functional and anatomical information collected in vivo onto cytoarchitectonic areas.
source: This allows projection of functional and anatomical information collected in vivo onto the cytoarchitectonic areas, which has the potential to contribute to the ongoing debate on the parcellation of the human auditory cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a potential application and contribution of the method.

claim: Various parcellation schemes have been proposed for the human auditory cortex, identifying primary, secondary belt, and tertiary parabelt auditory areas.
source: Historically, there has been a substantial effort to describe the micro-anatomy of the human auditory cortex (Von Economo and Horn, 1930; Galaburda and Sanides, 1980; Rivier and Clarke, 1997; Morosan et al., 2001; Wallace et al., 2002; Morosan et al., 2005; Clarke and Morosan, 2012; Nieuwenhuys, 2013). Various parcellation schemes have been proposed, which identify a primary area (core; primary auditory cortex) as well as secondary belt and tertiary parabelt auditory areas (Rivier and Clarke, 1997; Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: The primary auditory cortex (PAC) is generally located on the medial two-thirds of Heschl's Gyrus.
source: The primary auditory cortex (PAC) is generally located on the medial two-thirds of Heschl's Gyrus.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Classical cyto- and myelo-architectural approaches are limited by the absence of an objective metric defining cytoarchitectonic areas.
source: It has proven challenging to use these results to identify auditory areas in individuals in vivo, as classical cyto- (and myelo-) architectural approaches are limited by the absence of an objective metric defining cytoarchitectonic areas.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of classical approaches.

claim: Relating micro-anatomical characteristics to macro-anatomy is hampered by the inherent two-dimensional representation of results and scarce information regarding inter-subject variability.
source: In addition, relating micro-anatomical characteristics to macro-anatomy is hampered by the inherent two-dimensional representation of the results (i.e. by means of drawings or labeled slices) and scarce information regarding inter-subject variability.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a challenge in the field.

claim: Observer-independent methods for the analysis of serial cytoarchitectonically stained sections that correct for shrinkage artifacts have been developed in the last 20 years.
source: Instead, observer-independent methods for the analysis of serial cytoarchitectonically stained sections, that additionally correct for shrinkage artifacts typical of histological processing (Amunts et al., 2000), have been developed in the last 20 years (Schleicher et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Morosan et al., 2001 identified various auditory areas in the superior temporal cortex and generated a probabilistic atlas based on 10 individual brains.
source: Using this method, Morosan et al., 2001 identified various auditory areas in the superior temporal cortex and generated a probabilistic atlas based on 10 individual brains.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The probabilistic atlas allows assigning probabilistic values to in vivo brain images.
source: This atlas (Eickhoff et al., 2005) allows assigning probabilistic values to in vivo brain images and has been used to, for example, validate the delineation of PAC on the basis of in vivo MRI images whose contrast is related to myelin (Dick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The probabilistic atlas is generated using a volume registration method.
source: The probabilistic atlas is generated using a volume registration method.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of the existing atlas.

claim: There is exceptionally reliable correspondence between micro- and macro-anatomy in many cortical areas.
source: Instead, the exceptionally reliable correspondence between micro- and macro-anatomy known to be present in many cortical areas (Turner, 2013) has inspired the use of registration methods that rely on cortical surfaces and macro-anatomical landmarks such as the major gyri and sulci (i.e. curvature-based alignment [CBA] rather than the whole volumetric data [Fischl et al., 1999; Frost and Goebel, 2012; Goebel et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Surface-based alignment methods have been shown to improve the accuracy of inter-individual registration in micro-anatomically defined primary motor cortex.
source: Surface-based alignment methods have been shown to improve the accuracy of inter-individual registration in micro-anatomically defined primary motor cortex (Fischl, 2013), the human middle temporal area (hMT) (Frost and Goebel, 2013), and to improve the registration of a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the ventral visual system (Rosenke et al., 2018; Fischl et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Surface-based alignment methods improve the registration of the human middle temporal area (hMT).
source: Surface-based alignment methods have been shown to improve the accuracy of inter-individual registration in micro-anatomically defined primary motor cortex (Fischl, 2013), the human middle temporal area (hMT) (Frost and Goebel, 2013), and to improve the registration of a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the ventral visual system (Rosenke et al., 2018; Fischl et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Surface-based alignment methods improve the registration of a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the ventral visual system.
source: Surface-based alignment methods have been shown to improve the accuracy of inter-individual registration in micro-anatomically defined primary motor cortex (Fischl, 2013), the human middle temporal area (hMT) (Frost and Goebel, 2013), and to improve the registration of a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the ventral visual system (Rosenke et al., 2018; Fischl et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: CBA is routinely used in studies investigating the functional and anatomical properties of auditory cortical areas with the aim of minimizing inter-individual variability.
source: With the aim of minimizing inter-individual variability and thus improving (statistical) power when mapping functional properties, CBA is also routinely used in studies investigating the functional and anatomical properties of auditory cortical areas.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as current practice in the field.

claim: Local landmark alignment approaches have been used for aligning temporal cortical regions.
source: Beyond the use of whole brain curvature patterns, local landmark alignment approaches have also been used for aligning temporal cortical regions (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Local landmark alignment methods have been shown to outperform approaches that optimize whole brain features based on their ability to obtain clearer gyral and sulcal structures and higher resolution functional maps at the group level.
source: These methods have been shown to outperform approaches that optimize whole brain features on the basis of both their ability to obtain clearer gyral and sulcal structures as well as higher resolution functional maps at the group level.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from previous research.

claim: Heschl's Gyrus substantially varies in shape across individuals and across hemispheres.
source: However, Heschl's Gyrus substantially varies in shape across individuals and across hemispheres, and slight changes in the primary auditory cortex location have been reported in subjects with a typical morphological variation of the Heschl's Gyrus (Heschl, 1878; Rademacher et al., 1993; Hackett et al., 2001; Marie et al., 2015.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Slight changes in the primary auditory cortex location have been reported in subjects with typical morphological variation of Heschl's Gyrus.
source: However, Heschl's Gyrus substantially varies in shape across individuals and across hemispheres, and slight changes in the primary auditory cortex location have been reported in subjects with a typical morphological variation of the Heschl's Gyrus (Heschl, 1878; Rademacher et al., 1993; Hackett et al., 2001; Marie et al., 2015.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: It is debatable if curvature-based alignment improves the correspondence of micro-anatomically defined auditory areas and their corresponding functional characteristics given the variation in superior temporal plane macro-anatomy.
source: Given this variation in superior temporal plane macro-anatomy across individuals and shift of micro-anatomical areas with macro-anatomy, it is debatable if curvature-based alignment (either based on whole brain or local landmarks) improves the correspondence of micro-anatomically defined auditory areas and their corresponding functional characteristics.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the motivation for the study.

claim: The study applied curvature based alignment (CBA) and a procedure tailored to the temporal lobe by incorporating anatomical priors (CBA+).
source: To address this issue, here we applied curvature based alignment (abbreviated as CBA), as well as a procedure tailored to the temporal lobe by incorporating anatomical priors (abbreviated as CBA+).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the approach taken in the study.

claim: The study aimed at justifying the use of CBA or CBA+ in functional studies of the temporal lobe by evaluating the inter-individual alignment resulting from these procedures.
source: By evaluating the inter-individual alignment resulting from these procedures (and comparing them to the original volumetric approach), we aimed at justifying the use of CBA or CBA+ in functional studies of the temporal lobe.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the goal of the study.

claim: The study reconstructed cortical surfaces from the data of Morosan et al., 2001.
source: In particular, we reconstructed cortical surfaces from the data of Morosan et al., 2001 and investigated the effect that maximizing macro-anatomical inter-individual alignment has on the overlap of micro-anatomically defined auditory cortical areas.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the methodology.

claim: A method that provides a more accurate inter-individual alignment of postmortem cytoarchitecture will consequently provide a more accurate alignment of the associated functional properties.
source: We reasoned that a method that provides a more accurate inter-individual alignment of (postmortem) cytoarchitecture will consequently provide a more accurate alignment of the associated functional properties.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the reasoning behind the study.

claim: The study validates the use of CBA in previous studies.
source: Thereby, here we validate the use of CBA in previous studies and demonstrate that CBA+ is a better tool for aligning the superior temporal plane across participants.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as one of the contributions of the study.

claim: CBA+ is a better tool for aligning the superior temporal plane across participants than CBA.
source: Thereby, here we validate the use of CBA in previous studies and demonstrate that CBA+ is a better tool for aligning the superior temporal plane across participants.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: The study provides an improved probabilistic surface atlas of auditory cortical regions as a publicly available resource.
source: Moreover, we provide an improved probabilistic surface atlas of auditory cortical regions as a publicly available resource for the auditory community (Gulban, 2020; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/cortical-auditory-atlas).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a contribution of the study.

claim: The study applied CBA+ to an in vivo dataset collected at 7 Tesla.
source: We showcase this approach by applying CBA+ to an in vivo dataset collected at 7 Tesla and projecting the improved cytoarchitectonic atlas onto functional and anatomical group maps.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an application of the method.

claim: The study aligned the cytoarchitectonic atlas and in vivo data to a recent temporal lobe parcellation based on in vivo measurements from Glasser et al., 2016.
source: In addition, in order to contribute to the ongoing debate on the in vivo localization of auditory cortical areas (Moerel et al., 2014; Besle et al., 2018), we align the cytoarchitectonic atlas (and in vivo data) to a recent temporal lobe parcellation based on in vivo measurements (Glasser et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the study's approach.

claim: The study obtained cytoarchitectonically labeled temporal cortical areas and postmortem MR images of 10 brains volumetrically aligned to the Colin27 space.
source: We obtained cytoarchitectonically labeled temporal cortical areas and postmortem MR images of 10 brains (volumetrically aligned (rigid body) to the Colin27 space) used in the JuBrain cytoarchitectonic Atlas (Amunts and Zilles, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the data used in the study.

claim: The cytoarchitectonically labeled areas were TE 1.0, TE 1.1, TE 1.2, TE 2.1, TE 2.2, TE 3, STS 1, and STS 2.
source: The cytoarchitectonically labeled areas were TE 1.0, TE 1.1, and TE 1.2 from Morosan et al., 2001, TE 2.1 and TE 2.2 from Clarke and Morosan, 2012, TE three from Morosan et al., 2005, and STS one and STS two from Zachlod et al., 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: The white matter - gray matter boundary was segmented in all 10 postmortem brains to perform cortex based alignment.
source: In order to perform cortex based alignment, the white matter - gray matter boundary was segmented in all 10 postmortem brains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as part of the methodology.

claim: A combination of image filtering techniques and a histogram-based segmentation approach was used to obtain the segmentation, which reduced the amount of required manual corrections.
source: To obtain this segmentation, we have used a combination of image filtering techniques and a histogram-based segmentation approach (Gulban et al., 2018b), which reduced the amount of required manual corrections (see Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as part of the methodology.

claim: Cortical surfaces were reconstructed to perform three different types of group alignment methods: rigid body, CBA, and CBA+.
source: Cortical surfaces were reconstructed to perform three different types of group alignment methods. These methods were rigid body (i.e. considering surface sampling [compared to volumentric alignment] and rigid body registration), CBA and CBA with anatomical priors (CBA+; including the anterior Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus, the superior temporal sulcus, and the middle temporal gyrus as anatomical priors).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the methods compared in the study.

claim: CBA+ includes the anterior Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus, the superior temporal sulcus, and the middle temporal gyrus as anatomical priors.
source: These methods were rigid body (i.e. considering surface sampling [compared to volumentric alignment] and rigid body registration), CBA and CBA with anatomical priors (CBA+; including the anterior Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus, the superior temporal sulcus, and the middle temporal gyrus as anatomical priors).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the definition of CBA+.

claim: The surface approaches were compared to the original volumetric alignment in the Colin27 space.
source: We additionally compared these surface approaches to the original volumetric alignment in the Colin27 space.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as part of the comparison.

claim: The performance of the alignment methods was validated by comparing the overlap between cytoarchitectonic areas across individuals.
source: We have validated the performance of these methods by comparing the overlap between cytoarchitectonic areas across individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the validation approach.

claim: CBA+ was used to create superior temporal cortical group maps of in vivo MRI measurements at 7T.
source: We subsequently used CBA+ to create superior temporal cortical group maps of in vivo MRI (at 7T) measurements and to align them to the probabilistic cytoarchitectonic atlas.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an application of CBA+.

claim: The increased sharpness of the average curvature maps indicates improved correspondence of macro-anatomical features in CBA and CBA+ compared to rigid only alignment in the temporal lobe.
source: In the temporal lobe, the increased sharpness of the average curvature maps indicates the improved correspondence of the macro-anatomical features in CBA and CBA+ compared to the rigid only alignment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1.

claim: An improvement of CBA+ over standard CBA is noticeable at the level of the Heschl's Gyrus in the right hemisphere.
source: Especially in the right hemisphere (third row in Figure 1), an improvement of CBA+ over standard CBA is noticeable at the level of the Heschl's Gyrus (indicated by a red circle).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The improvement in alignment of the macro-anatomical features in the temporal lobes is visible when considering the folded average meshes of the ten brains in the postmortem dataset.
source: The improvement in alignment of the macro-anatomical features in the temporal lobes (left and right) is also visible when considering the folded average meshes of the ten brains in the postmortem dataset (i.e. average folded meshes, Figure 1 rows 2 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Improved alignment should increase the 3D complexity of the average folded mesh in absence of large macro-anatomical differences across individuals.
source: In absence of large macro-anatomical differences across the individuals, improved alignment should increase the 3D complexity (e.g. gyri and sulci appearing very clearly distinguishable) of the average folded mesh.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an expected outcome of improved alignment.

claim: The number of Heschl's Gyri varied in the postmortem sample: 1, 1.5, and 2 Heschl's Gyri were observed in 5, 4, and 1 right hemispheres respectively, and 6, 2, and 2 left hemispheres respectively.
source: In particular, we observed 1, 1.5 and 2 Heschl's Gyri in [5, 4, and 1, respectively] right hemispheres and [6, 2, and 2, respectively] left hemispheres.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Three hemispheres (one right and two left) had a single Heschl's Gyrus that was continuous at the anterior part of the anterior temporal convolution, resulting in a split superior temporal gyrus.
source: Second, we observed the presence of three hemispheres (one right and two left ones) whose single Heschl's Gyrus was continuous at the anterior part of the anterior temporal convolution, resulting in a split superior temporal gyrus (i.e. interrupted by an intermediate sulcus between the anterior and posterior part with respect to the location of the Heschl's Gyrus - Figure 13 lower right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 13.

claim: The rare morphological pattern of a split superior temporal gyrus was first described in Heschl, 1878 and was reported to occur in approximately 10% of all brains inspected by Richard L. Heschl (110 of 1087 brains).
source: This rare morphological pattern was first described in Heschl, 1878 and was reported to occur % 10 of all brains inspected by Richard L. Heschl (110 of 1087 brains).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The split superior temporal gyrus pattern was approximately eight times more likely to occur on the left hemisphere compared to the right.
source: It was 1̃eight times more likely to occur on the left hemisphere in comparison to right (also see Rademacher et al., 1993), for another reference to Heschl's work in English).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The tailored alignment (CBA+) results in a more prominently defined Heschl's Gyrus in the average mesh.
source: As expected, the tailored alignment we developed here results in a more prominently defined Heschl's Gyrus in the average mesh, resulting from the correct alignment of the anterior Heschl's Gyrus across individual hemispheres.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an outcome of CBA+.

claim: In split superior temporal gyrus cases, the gyrus was defined as continuous (bridging the intermediate sulcus).
source: In the split superior temporal gyrus cases, we defined the gyrus as continuous (i.e. bridging the intermediate sulcus).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological decision.

claim: The definition of the split superior temporal gyrus as continuous did not compromise the alignment of the anterior Heschl's Gyrus.
source: While this definition did not compromise the alignment of the anterior Heschl's Gyrus, the impact of the approach we followed in the alignment of regions in proximity to the intermediate sulcus would require a larger sample on which to evaluate alignment separately according to this macro-anatomical variation (i.e. aligning separately individuals with a split/continuous superior temporal gyrus).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation and limitation.

claim: For all cytoarchitectonic areas, CBA+ improves the overlap as indicated by the increased probability of a vertex to be labeled as belonging to same area across the ten brains.
source: For all cytoarchitectonic areas, CBA+ improves the overlap (as indicated by the increased probability of a vertex to be labeled as belonging to same area across the ten brains).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figures 2-7.

claim: Both the histograms and the dice coefficients indicate that for the cytoarchitectonic areas along Heschl's Gyrus (Te1.0, Te1.1 and Te1.2), the largest overlap is provided by CBA+.
source: Both the histograms and the dice coefficients indicate that, for the cytoarchitectonic areas along Heschl's Gyrus (Te1.0, Te1.1 and Te1.2), the largest overlap is provided by CBA+, which improves micro-anatomical correspondence compared to the volume-based alignment and the two other surface approaches we evaluated.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figures 8, 9 and Tables 1, 2.

claim: For the areas in the planum temporale (Te2.1 and Te2.2), all surface approaches improve micro-anatomical correspondence compared to the volume alignment, and CBA+ provides an additional benefit especially for the area Te2.1.
source: For the areas in the planum temporale (Te2.1 and Te2.2), all surface approaches improve micro-anatomical correspondence compared to the volume alignment, and CBA+ provides an additional benefit especially for the area Te2.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data.

claim: For the areas in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus and middle temporal gyrus (Te3, STS1 and STS2), all surface approaches improve micro-anatomical correspondence compared to the volume alignment while differences between standard CBA and CBA+ are modest.
source: Similarly, for the areas in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus and middle temporal gyrus (Te3, STS1 and STS2), all surface approaches improve micro-anatomical correspondence compared to the volume alignment while differences between standard CBA and CBA+ are modest.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data.

claim: CBA+ was used to produce an average morphology for the in vivo data.
source: First, we used CBA+ to produce an average morphology for the in vivo data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as part of the analysis of in vivo data.

claim: The alignment allowed derivation of group level maps based on the available anatomical and functional data.
source: This alignment allowed us to derive group level maps based on the available anatomical and functional data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an outcome of the alignment.

claim: Anatomical MRI data (0.7 mm isotropic) were used to derive intra cortical contrast related to myelin from the division of T1w and T2*w data.
source: In particular, anatomical MRI data (0.7 mm isotropic) were used to derive intra cortical contrast related to myelin from the division of T1w and T2*w data.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as part of the analysis.

claim: Functional MRI data (1.1 mm isotropic) collected by presenting natural sounds and analyzed with an fMRI encoding approach were used to derive tonotopic maps.
source: In addition, functional MRI data (1.1 mm isotropic) collected by presenting natural sounds and analyzed with an fMRI encoding approach (Moerel et al., 2012), were used to derive tonotopic maps (see Figure 10 - Supplement Figures to Figure 10 report all the individual maps).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: CBA+ was used to align the average morphology of the in vivo data to the cytoarchitectonic atlas.
source: Second, using CBA+, we aligned the average morphology of the in vivo data to the cytoarchitectonic atlas.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as part of the analysis.

claim: Aligning the in vivo data to the cytoarchitectonic atlas allowed projection of cytoarchitectonic parcels on the in vivo maps and evaluation of their relationship.
source: This allowed us to project cytoarchitectonic parcels on the in vivo maps and evaluate their relationship.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an outcome of the alignment.

claim: Intra cortical contrast related to myelin highlights the medial Heschl's Gyrus as the most myelinated region in the temporal cortex.
source: Intra cortical contrast related to myelin highlights the (medial) Heschl's Gyrus as the most myelinated region in the temporal cortex (see Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: Across cytoarchitectonic areas, Te1.0 shows the highest myelination contrast.
source: Across cytoarchitectonic areas, Te1.0 shows the highest myelination contrast.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: The average tonotopic pattern highlights the Heschl's Gyrus as preferring low frequencies for the most part, while surrounding areas prefer high frequencies.
source: The average tonotopic pattern highlights the Heschl's Gyrus as, for the most part, preferring low frequencies, while surrounding areas (in posterior antero-medial and antero-lateral directions) prefer high frequencies (see Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: The high-frequency areas form an inverted 'V' pattern surrounding the Heschl's Gyrus.
source: The high-frequency areas form an inverted 'V' pattern surrounding the Heschl's Gyrus (Da Costa et al., 2011; Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Cytoarchitectonic primary cortical areas (Te1) cover the Heschl's Gyrus, with the core (Te1.0) in its middle section which at the group level appears characterized by mainly low-frequency preference.
source: Cytoarchitectonic primary cortical areas (Te1) cover the Heschl's Gyrus, with the core (Te1.0) in its middle section which (at the group level) appears characterized by mainly low-frequency preference (see Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claim: Area Te1.1, located medial to Te1.0, may reflect an intermediate processing stage between primary and belt areas and covers one tonotopic gradient going from high to low in an antero-medial to postero-lateral direction.
source: Located medial to Te1.0, area Te1.1 may reflect an intermediate processing stage between primary and belt areas (Moerel et al., 2014) and covers one tonotopic gradient going from high to low in an antero-medial to postero-lateral direction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: Te2.2 covers a posterior portion of the tonotopic gradient running in the posterior to anterior direction.
source: Te2.2 covers a posterior portion of the tonotopic gradient running in the posterior to anterior direction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Te2.1, covering an intermediate location between Te2.2 and Te1.0/Te1.2, overlaps with a low-frequency preferring region in the lateral portion of the Heschl's sulcus.
source: Te2.1, covering an intermediate location between Te2.2 and Te1.0/Te1.2, overlaps with a low-frequency preferring region in the lateral portion of the Heschl's sulcus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Te3 covers a low-frequency portion of the tonotopic maps along the superior temporal gyrus.
source: Finally, Te3 covers a low-frequency portion of the tonotopic maps along the superior temporal gyrus (Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The superior temporal plane shows considerable macro-anatomical variability across individuals.
source: The superior temporal plane shows considerable macro-anatomical variability across individuals (Pfeifer, 1921; Pfeifer, 1936; Von Economo and Horn, 1930; Rademacher et al., 1993; Zoellner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Large inter-individual differences in the superior temporal plane are detrimental to functional and anatomical in vivo investigations of the temporal lobe if unaccounted for.
source: If unaccounted for, these large inter-individual differences are detrimental to functional (and anatomical) in vivo investigations of the temporal lobe as they limit the efficacy of alignment procedures that are used in group studies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a consequence of variability.

claim: When signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is limited, investigators rely on averaging functional and anatomical information both within a subject and across subjects.
source: In addition, when signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is limited, investigators rely on averaging functional (and anatomical) information, both within a subject (i.e. within a cortical area across voxels) and across subjects.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as current practice in the field.

claim: Functional and anatomical localizers exist for some cortical regions in the temporal lobe (e.g., PAC, voice regions).
source: While functional and anatomical localizers exist for some cortical regions in the temporal lobe (e.g., PAC -Moerel et al., 2012; voice regions - Belin et al., 2000), such localizers are not available for the majority of the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Localizers are not available for the majority of the auditory cortex.
source: While functional and anatomical localizers exist for some cortical regions in the temporal lobe (e.g., PAC -Moerel et al., 2012; voice regions - Belin et al., 2000), such localizers are not available for the majority of the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation in the field.

claim: Investigators often rely on available parcellations which result from postmortem or in vivo investigations in a population.
source: As a consequence, investigators often rely on available parcellations (see, e.g., the procedure followed by Dick et al., 2012) which result from postmortem (or in vivo) investigations in a population and as a consequence rely on the quality of the inter-subject alignment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: The study used 10 individual brains available from the JuBrain cytoarchitectonic Atlas.
source: We have used 10 individual brains available from the JuBrain cytoarchitectonic Atlas (The JuBrain atlas is available through the Atlas of the Human Brain Project https://jubrain.fz-juelich.de/ (Amunts and Zilles, 2015) together with a surface registration method that minimizes macro-anatomical variability around the transverse temporal gyrus (similar to Rosenke et al., 2018) to show that minimizing macro-anatomical variability in the superior temporal plane results in improved micro-anatomical correspondence across brains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: Minimizing macro-anatomical variability in the superior temporal plane results in improved micro-anatomical correspondence across brains.
source: We have used 10 individual brains available from the JuBrain cytoarchitectonic Atlas (The JuBrain atlas is available through the Atlas of the Human Brain Project https://jubrain.fz-juelich.de/ (Amunts and Zilles, 2015) together with a surface registration method that minimizes macro-anatomical variability around the transverse temporal gyrus (similar to Rosenke et al., 2018) to show that minimizing macro-anatomical variability in the superior temporal plane results in improved micro-anatomical correspondence across brains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding of the study.

claim: The study provides a more accurate probabilistic atlas of the cytoarchitectonic areas in the temporal lobe.
source: Our results have two potential benefits for the auditory neuroscience community. First, by providing a more accurate (i.e. with improved inter subject alignment) probabilistic atlas of the cytoarchitectonic areas in the temporal lobe, we provide a valuable resource for those studies that rely on a parcellation scheme.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a contribution of the study.

claim: Minimizing a particular set of macro-anatomical features results in a more accurate micro-anatomical alignment.
source: Second, we show that minimizing a particular set of macro-anatomical features results in a more accurate micro-anatomical alignment, and thus that using local landmarks for aligning temporal regions results in a better alignment of cytoarchitectonic areas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding of the study.

claim: Using local landmarks for aligning temporal regions results in a better alignment of cytoarchitectonic areas.
source: Second, we show that minimizing a particular set of macro-anatomical features results in a more accurate micro-anatomical alignment, and thus that using local landmarks for aligning temporal regions results in a better alignment of cytoarchitectonic areas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding of the study.

claim: The study justifies the use of local landmark approaches when aligning individual temporal cortices with each other or to a template.
source: This justifies the use of these approaches (the one we propose here or others that have been proposed before Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005) when aligning individual temporal cortices with each other (or to a template).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Applying a surface registration for inter-subject alignment required accurate segmentation of the postmortem MRI dataset.
source: Applying a surface registration for inter-subject alignment required accurate segmentation of the postmortem MRI dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a methodological requirement.

claim: The available 10 brains showed typical variations in the morphology of the Heschl's Gyrus, with a single Heschl's Gyrus being the most prevalent.
source: The availabe 10 brains showed typical variations in the morphology of the Heschl's Gyrus (with a single Heschl's Gyrus being the most prevalent one), as well as cases in which the Heschl's Gyrus was continuous to the anterior portion of the superior temporal gyrus (Heschl, 1878).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: Standard CBA minimizes macro-anatomical variation across subjects across the whole brain in a coarse to fine iterative approach.
source: The standard approach minimizes macro-anatomical variation across subjects (i.e. maximizes the overlap of the curvature maps) across the whole brain (in a coarse to fine iterative approach).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of standard CBA.

claim: Standard CBA is driven by the major anatomical landmarks including the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus.
source: As such, standard CBA is driven by the major anatomical landmarks including the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of standard CBA.

claim: Standard CBA can result in compromised alignment of smaller but consistent anatomical features such as the Heschl's Gyrus.
source: This, however, can result in compromised alignment of smaller (but consistent) anatomical features such as the Heschl's Gyrus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of standard CBA.

claim: The necessity to use local landmarks to guide the alignment of temporal regions has been considered in previous research.
source: For this reason, here we have considered the application of an approach tailored to the superior temporal plane. The necessity to use local landmarks to guide the alignment of temporal regions has been considered in previous research (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Previous approaches defined macro-anatomical points or lines covering the main gyri and sulci in the temporal cortex for alignment.
source: By defining macro-anatomical points in the temporal cortex (Kang et al., 2004) or lines covering the main gyri and sulci (Desai et al., 2005) both linear and non-linear alignment procedures have been compared to global spherical alignment and volumetric approaches.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The study provided additional landmarks (the Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus) to the CBA procedure.
source: Here, we provided additional landmarks (the Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus) to the CBA procedure and, differently from previous approaches (that considered only the local landmarks when aligning the temporal cortex), we optimized alignment of both local and global macro-anatomical features.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the approach taken in the study.

claim: The study optimized alignment of both local and global macro-anatomical features, differently from previous approaches that considered only local landmarks.
source: Here, we provided additional landmarks (the Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus) to the CBA procedure and, differently from previous approaches (that considered only the local landmarks when aligning the temporal cortex), we optimized alignment of both local and global macro-anatomical features.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a distinction from previous approaches.

claim: CBA+ improved the alignment across subjects in the superior temporal cortex compared to standard CBA.
source: By doing so, we improved the alignment across subjects in the superior temporal cortex (see e.g. the difference in the average curvature maps between standard CBA and CBA+ in Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both CBA and CBA+ greatly improved the macro-anatomical correspondence when compared to a rigid body procedure.
source: Both the CBA and CBA+ approach greatly improved the macro-anatomical correspondence when compared to a rigid body procedure (which by sampling the volumetric data on surfaces already offers an improvement compared to the original volumetric alignment - see Figure 8 and Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The result of improved macro-anatomical correspondence with CBA and CBA+ is in line with previously reported increased macro-anatomical correspondence obtained when using alignment procedures that use local landmarks.
source: This result is in line with the previously reported increased macro-anatomical correspondence obtained when using alignment procedures that use local landmarks (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The advantage of the tailored approach (CBA+) is stronger in the right hemisphere, with some residual misalignment for the left Heschl's Gyrus.
source: The advantage of the tailored approach (CBA+, rightmost column in Figure 1) is stronger in the right hemisphere, with some residual misalignment for the left Heschl's Gyrus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The difference in performance between hemispheres could be explained by the larger prevalence in the left hemisphere of cases with the Heschl's Gyrus merging with the anterior portion of the superior temporal gyrus (split superior temporal gyrus cases).
source: This difference in performance could be explained by the larger prevalence (within our sample) in the left hemisphere of cases with the Heschl's Gyrus merging with the anterior portion of the superior temporal gyrus (i.e. split superior temporal gyrus cases; two in the left and one in the right hemisphere).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possible explanation.

claim: A larger sample could allow evaluating the impact of the split superior temporal gyrus variation on alignment by evaluating alignment separately with and without such cases.
source: In the future, a larger sample could allow evaluating this issue, as well as the impact that the inclusion of this macro-anatomical variation has on the alignment of regions close to the superior temporal gyrus, by evaluating the alignment separately (with and without) such cases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claim: Tailoring the alignment of the temporal lobe to local landmarks is motivated by the expectation that minimizing macro-anatomy will result in improved micro-anatomical alignment.
source: Tailoring the alignment of the temporal lobe to local landmarks is motivated by the expectation that minimizing macro-anatomy will consequently result in improved micro-anatomical alignment (i.e. the alignment of cortical areas in the temporal lobe) and that this in turn improves functional alignment (assuming that function and micro-anatomy co-localize).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the motivation for the approach.

claim: Previous studies have shown that approaches that use local landmarks result in improved group functional activation.
source: While previous studies have shown that approaches that use local landmarks result in improved group functional activation (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005), here we addressed the much required validation of how well such an approach reduces the underlying micro-anatomical variability.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Improving macro-anatomical correspondence resulted in improved overlap of the cytoarchitectonic areas across subjects.
source: Improving macro-anatomical correspondence resulted in improved overlap of the cytoarchitectonic areas across subjects.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding.

claim: As a result of CBA+ alignment, the micro-anatomically defined areas were smaller and the probability for a vertex to be labeled as belonging to the same area across the postmortem samples was higher.
source: As a result of the CBA+ alignment, the micro-anatomically defined areas were smaller and the probability for a vertex to be labeled as belonging to the same area across the postmortem samples was higher (see Figures 2–7 and the histograms in Figure 8 and Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figures 2-9.

claim: The tailored approach (CBA+) resulted in increased overlap in all areas but especially in those on Heschl's Gyrus or immediately adjacent to it (Te1.0, Te1.1, Te1.2 and Te2.1).
source: The tailored approach (CBA+) resulted in increased overlap (also compared to standard CBA) in all areas but especially in those on Heschl's Gyrus or immediately adjacent to it (Te1.0, Te1.1, Te1.2 and Te2.1 - see Table 1 and Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The increased overlap in areas on or adjacent to Heschl's Gyrus is a direct consequence of defining the most anterior Heschl's Gyrus as an additional landmark for alignment.
source: This result is a direct consequence of defining the (most anterior) Heschl's Gyrus as an additional landmark for alignment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for the result.

claim: The most anterior Heschl's Gyrus was recognized as the putative location of primary auditory cortex in the case of a complete duplication on the basis of myelo-architecture.
source: The most anterior Heschl's Gyrus was recognized as the putative location of primary auditory cortex in the case of a complete duplication on the basis of myelo-architecture (Hackett et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: When the most anterior Heschl's Gyrus is not used as a landmark, the duplication of the Heschl's Gyrus results in poorer matching across subjects.
source: When this anatomical landmark is not used, the duplication of the Heschl's Gyrus results in poorer matching across subjects (i.e. the most posterior duplication of some subjects is aligned to the single Heschl's Gyrus of other subjects).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for the importance of the landmark.

claim: The postmortem dataset includes six Heschl's Gyrus duplication cases (four in the right and two in the left hemisphere).
source: The postmortem dataset includes six Heschl's Gyrus duplication cases (four in the right and two in the left hemisphere).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of the dataset.

claim: Follow-up studies are needed to evaluate the effect of an incomplete duplication of Heschl's Gyrus.
source: Follow-up studies are needed to evaluate the effect of an incomplete duplication of Heschl's Gyrus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claim: Previous myelo-architecture studies reported a shift of primary areas toward the intermediate Heschl's sulcus in the case of an incomplete duplication.
source: As previous myelo-architecture studies reported a shift of primary areas toward the intermediate Heschl's sulcus in the case of an incomplete duplication (Hackett et al., 2001), a partial alignment of the primary areas (Te1.0 and Te1.1) may be expected.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: Examining the effect of an incomplete duplication on micro-anatomical alignment may provide additional insights for further refinement of the alignment procedure.
source: Examining the effect of an incomplete duplication on micro-anatomical alignment may provide additional insights for a further refinement of the alignment procedure we propose here.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claim: Areas along the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus landmarks were also better realigned by CBA+, though to a lesser degree than areas on Heschl's Gyrus.
source: In addition to the anterior Heschl's Gyrus, CBA+ includes the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus as anatomical landmarks. While to a lesser degree than the areas on Heschl's Gyrus, areas along these landmarks were also better realigned by CBA+.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: Favoring the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus with respect to other major landmarks on the cortex is beneficial for the alignment of temporal areas.
source: This indicates that favoring these gyri/sulci with respect to other major landmarks on the cortex is beneficial for the alignment of temporal areas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the results.

claim: The improved cytoarchitectonic overlap obtained with CBA+ suggests that this approach may be relevant for the functional and anatomical investigation of auditory temporal areas in vivo.
source: The improved cytoarchitectonic overlap obtained with CBA+ suggests that this approach may be relevant for the functional and anatomical investigation of (auditory) temporal areas in vivo, as well as the investigation (postmortem and in vivo ) of other cortical regions in which macro-anatomical variability is high.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion and suggestion.

claim: The study makes the individual hemisphere surface models and the individual cytoarchitectonic areas publicly available.
source: We make the individual hemisphere surface models and the individual cytoarchitectonic areas used in this study publicly available at https://kg.ebrains.eu/search/instances/Dataset/ff71a4d1-ea14-4ed6-898e-b92d95b3c446.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a contribution of the study.

claim: The publicly available dataset could be used to compare the performance of different landmark based approaches and non-linear volumetric approaches to CBA+.
source: In follow-up investigations, this publicly available data set could also be used to compare the performance of different landmark based approaches that use only local landmarks (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005) as well as non-linear volumetric approaches to CBA+.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claim: The study applied CBA+ to align anatomical and functional data collected at 7 Tesla across individuals.
source: To showcase the application of CBA+ to the analysis of in vivo MRI data, we applied the same procedure to align anatomical and functional data collected at 7 Tesla across individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an application of the method.

claim: The pattern of myelin related intra cortical contrast followed previous reports.
source: The pattern of myelin related intra cortical contrast followed previous reports (Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Dick et al., 2012; De Martino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The alignment to the cytoarchitectonic atlas shows a high myelin-related contrast in area Te1.0, in agreement with previous studies.
source: The alignment to the cytoarchitectonic atlas shows a high myelin-related contrast in area Te1.0, in agreement with previous studies (Dick et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: A more clear cut separation between Te1.0 and Te1.1 may require the evaluation of myelin-related contrast across depths.
source: While subtle differences between Te1.0 and Te1.1 were already noticeable, a more clear cut separation between these regions may require the evaluation of myelin-related contrast across depths similarly to previous approaches (Dick et al., 2012; De Martino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claim: Future investigations may evaluate the information provided by intra anatomical contrast resulting from in vivo MRI acquisitions other than the one considered in the study.
source: In addition, future investigations may evaluate the information provided by intra anatomical contrast resulting from in vivo MRI acquisitions other than the one we considered here (e.g. using the orientation of intra-cortical fibers [McNab et al., 2013; Gulban et al., 2018a]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claim: The group tonotopy maps derived from the in vivo data follow previous reports.
source: The group tonotopy maps we derived from the in vivo data follow previous reports (Dick et al., 2012; Moerel et al., 2014; Besle et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The group tonotopy maps show one gradient within area Te1.1 progressing from high to low frequencies in antero-medial to postero-lateral direction.
source: In particular, they show one gradient within area Te1.1 progressing from high to low frequencies in antero-medial to postero-lateral direction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: Based on the average maps, a full tonotopic gradient was not visible in Te1.0, which was corresponding mainly with the low frequency area on medial Heschl's Gyrus.
source: Based on the average maps, a full tonotopic gradient was not visible in Te1.0, which was corresponding mainly with the low frequency area on medial Heschl's Gyrus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: The pattern in Te1.0 may be the result of excessive smoothing caused by inter-subject averaging that highlights the larger frequency gradient progressing in the anterior-posterior direction on the planum temporale.
source: This pattern may be the result of excessive smoothing caused by inter-subject averaging that highlights the larger frequency gradient that in tonotopic maps progresses in the anterior-posterior direction on the planum temporale and thus favors the interpretation of the pattern within larger cortical areas (Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possible explanation.

claim: Future studies are needed to quantify the information that can be leveraged from individual in vivo MRI data for characterizing the cytoarchitectonic areas.
source: While future studies are needed to quantify the information that can be leveraged from individual in vivo MRI data for characterizing the cytoarchitectonic areas, our preliminary results indicate that individual tonotopic [and myelin] maps (supplement figures to Figure 10) provide more fine grained information (within smaller areas such as e.g. Te1.0) (Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claim: Individual tonotopic and myelin maps provide more fine grained information within smaller areas such as Te1.0.
source: While future studies are needed to quantify the information that can be leveraged from individual in vivo MRI data for characterizing the cytoarchitectonic areas, our preliminary results indicate that individual tonotopic [and myelin] maps (supplement figures to Figure 10) provide more fine grained information (within smaller areas such as e.g. Te1.0) (Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 10 supplements.

claim: Te2.2 captured the most posterior portion of the larger tonotopic gradient that runs in a direction orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus.
source: Te2.2 captured the most posterior portion of the larger tonotopic gradient that, consistently with previous reports, we identify as running in a direction orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus (Moerel et al., 2014; Besle et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Te2.1 and Te3 covered low-frequency preferring regions of the tonotopic map in the lateral portion of the Heschl's sulcus and the superior temporal gyrus.
source: The other cytoarchitectonic regions that overlapped with our functional acquisition field of view (Te2.1 and Te3) covered low-frequency preferring regions of the tonotopic map in the lateral portion of the Heschl's sulcus and the superior temporal gyrus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: The results argue for the necessity of interpreting large-scale tonotopic maps, which by themselves do not allow defining the borders between superior temporal cortical areas.
source: These results argue for the necessity of interpreting large-scale tonotopic maps, which by themselves do not allow defining the borders between superior temporal cortical areas (Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: A large tonotopic gradient runs in a posterior to anterior direction.
source: A large tonotopic gradient unarguably runs in a posterior to anterior direction Da Costa et al., 2011; Besle et al., 2018.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: Equating the large posterior to anterior tonotopic gradient with the gradient that identifies the primary auditory cortex results in a view in which the core lies orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus.
source: Equating this gradient with the gradient that identifies the primary auditory cortex results in a view in which the core lies orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus (Da Costa et al., 2011; Saenz and Langers, 2014; Besle et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The cytoarchitectonic areas, now restricted in size by better aligning macro-anatomy, suggest that the auditory core (Te1) runs along Heschl's Gyrus (the 'classical' view).
source: On the other hand, the cytoarchitectonic areas -now restricted in size by better aligning macro-anatomy- suggest that the auditory core (Te1) runs along Heschl's Gyrus (i.e. the 'classical' view; Dick et al., 2012; Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The view that the auditory core runs along Heschl's Gyrus is strengthened by the combined interpretation of myelin and tonotopy as well as other auditory cortical functional characteristics.
source: This view is strengthened by the combined interpretation of myelin and tonotopy (see Figure 10 and results in Dick et al., 2012; Moerel et al., 2014) as well as other auditory cortical functional characteristics (e.g. frequency selectivity; Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations and shown in Figure 10.

claim: Interesting differences exist between the surface projection of the cytoarchitectonic areas compared to a recent parcellation of the temporal lobe derived solely from in vivo imaging (Glasser et al., 2016).
source: Interesting differences exist between the surface projection of the cytoarchitectonic areas compared to a recent parcellation of the temporal lobe derived solely from in vivo imaging (Glasser et al., 2016 - see Figure 11).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation and shown in Figure 11.

claim: Cytoarchitectonic areas Te1.1, Te1.0 and Te1.2 lie postero-medial to antero-lateral along the Heschl's Gyrus.
source: Cytoarchitectonic areas Te1.1, Te1.0 and Te1.2 lie postero-medial to antero-lateral along the Heschl's Gyrus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of the cytoarchitectonic areas.

claim: The most lateral subdivision (Te1.2) has been suggested to be the human homologue of area RT in the monkey (part of the auditory core) or part of the lateral belt.
source: The most lateral subdivision (Te1.2) has been suggested to be the human homologue of area RT in the monkey (and thus part of the auditory core) or part of the lateral belt (Moerel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: In the multi-modal MRI parcellation, Heschl's Gyrus is divided in an area labeled as A1, corresponding to the most medial two thirds, and its most lateral portion, which is part of the area labeled as the medial belt.
source: In the multi-modal MRI parcellation, on the other hand, Heschl's Gyrus is divided in an area labeled as A1, corresponding to the most medial two thirds, and its most lateral portion, which is part of the area labeled as the medial belt.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of the Glasser et al. parcellation.

claim: Outside of the Heschl's Gyrus, other differences between the in vivo and post-mortem atlas are visible.
source: Outside of the Heschl's Gyrus, other differences between the in vivo and post-mortem atlas are visible.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation.

claim: The lateral belt and parabelt areas as defined in the in vivo atlas occupy an area roughly corresponding to Te2, but the border between the areas labeled as belt and parabelt run approximately orthogonal to the border between Te2.1 and Te2.2.
source: The lateral belt and parabelt areas as defined in the in vivo atlas occupy an area roughly corresponding to Te2, but the border between the areas labeled as belt and parabelt run approximately orthogonal to the border between Te2.1 and Te2.2.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation of differences between atlases.

claim: Te3, previously considered as an homologue of parabelt, corresponds to the areas labeled as A4 and A5 in the in vivo atlas.
source: Te3, previously considered as an homologue of parabelt, corresponds to the areas labeled as A4 and A5 in the in vivo atlas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation of correspondence between atlases.

claim: STS1 overlaps with the dorsal portion of superior temporal sulcus (STSda and STSdp in the in vivo atlas) and STS2 with the ventral portion of superior temporal sulcus for the most part.
source: STS1 overlaps with the dorsal portion of superior temporal sulcus (STSda and STSdp in the in vivo atlas) and STS2 with the ventral portion of superior temporal sulcus for the most part.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation of correspondence between atlases.

claim: The differences between the cytoarchitectonic atlas and the in vivo multi modal atlas may be caused by an insufficient amount of information available in the in vivo data used for the parcellation of the superior temporal plane.
source: While the in vivo multi modal atlas has been derived from a large sample of participants (N = 210), these differences may be caused by an insufficient amount of information available in the in vivo data used for the parcellation of the superior temporal plane.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possible explanation for the differences.

claim: An alignment procedure tailored to the superior temporal cortex and driven by anatomical priors together with curvature improves inter-subject correspondence of cytoarchitectonic areas.
source: In conclusion, here we show that an alignment procedure tailored to the superior temporal cortex and driven by anatomical priors together with curvature improves inter-subject correspondence of cytoarchitectonic areas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Reducing macro-anatomical variability and improving cytoarchitectural correspondence may reduce the inter-subject variability of anatomical and functional characteristics probed in vivo.
source: Reducing macro-anatomical variability and improving cytoarchitectural correspondence may reduce the inter-subject variability of (anatomical and functional) characteristics probed in vivo, resulting in a more accurate definition of putative cortical (temporal) areas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion and implication of the study.

claim: The results go beyond the test case of 7 Tesla high-resolution data analysis and can benefit the auditory neuroscience community by justifying the use of a landmark based alignment approach when considering the temporal cortex.
source: These results go beyond the test case we provide here (the analysis of 7 Tesla high-resolution data) and can benefit the auditory neuroscience community as they justify the use of a landmark based alignment approach when considering the temporal cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the broader impact of the study.

claim: A landmark approach is expected to benefit studies that rely on inter individual alignment for statistical analysis.
source: In particular, we expect a landmark approach to benefit studies that rely on inter individual alignment for statistical analysis (as also already demonstrated by Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The improved anatomical cytoarchitectonic atlas is a resource for all investigations that rely on the definition of cytoarchitectonically defined regions of interest in their analyses.
source: In addition, the improved anatomical cytoarchitectonic atlas is a resource for all investigations (at both low and high fields) that rely on the definition of (cytoarchitectonically defined) regions of interest in their analyses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a contribution of the study.

claim: Having validated a landmark-based alignment justifies its use in investigations of the anatomical and functional characteristics of auditory cortical areas using in vivo MRI.
source: Finally, having validated a landmark-based alignment justifies its use in investigations of the anatomical and functional characteristics of auditory cortical areas using in vivo MRI.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion of the study.

claim: While demonstrated in the temporal cortex, the CBA+ approach is easily extendable to other cortical areas in which macro-anatomical inter subject variability is not easily accounted for by standard surface registration methods.
source: While we demonstrate its effectiveness in the temporal cortex, this approach is easily extendable to other cortical areas in which macro-anatomical inter subject variability is not easily accounted for by standard surface registration methods.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a broader application of the method.

claim: Future studies should evaluate if CBA+ is equally accurate for all known macro-anatomical variations of the morphology of the Heschl's Gyrus, apart from being more accurate.
source: Future studies should evaluate if this procedure, apart from being more accurate, is equally accurate for all known macro-anatomical variations of the morphology of the Heschl's Gyrus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.
